hints: Think about what a more positive $E^\circ$ value tells you about a species ability to gain electrons and act as an oxidant.
Recall the Data Booklet values for $\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-$ and link the direction of change to oxidising power.
walkthrough:
Link $E^\circ$ to oxidising power**
Picture the half reaction $\text{X}_2 + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{X}^-$. A more positive $E^\circ$ means that equilibrium lies further to the right, so $\text{X}_2$ picks up electrons more readily. That is exactly what a strong oxidant does, it oxidises others by itself being reduced.

Read the trend from the Data Booklet**
$\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^-$ is about $+1.36\text{ V}$, $\text{Br}_2/\text{Br}^-$ is about $+1.07\text{ V}$ and $\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-$ is about $+0.54\text{ V}$. The value falls, becoming less positive, going down Group 17.

State the reactivity conclusion**
Because the tendency to gain electrons falls, $\text{Cl}_2$ is the strongest oxidant and $\text{I}_2$ is the weakest. So oxidising strength decreases $\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$.

Final answer: The $E^\circ$ for $\text{X}_2/\text{X}^-$ becomes less positive down the group from $\text{Cl}_2$ to $\text{I}_2$.\nTherefore the halogens become less reactive as oxidising agents down the group.

hints: Remember chlorine with water undergoes disproportionation to oxidation states -1 and +1, so think of the two chlorine containing acids formed.
walkthrough:
Spot the disproportionation**
Chlorine starts at oxidation state 0. In water one atom is reduced to $\text{Cl}^-$ in $\text{HCl}$ where Cl is -1, and the other is oxidised to $\text{ClO}^-$ type species in $\text{HClO}$ where Cl is +1. Balancing atoms gives $\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \longrightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{HClO}$.

hints: Identify the two half cells that combine to give $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, one is $\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^-$ and the other involves $\text{ClO}^-$.
Use $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ$ (more positive half cell) minus $E^\circ$ (less positive half cell) with $+1.36\text{ V}$ and $+0.89\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Pick out the two $E^\circ$ values**
From the Data Booklet, the reduction $\text{Cl}_2 + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Cl}^-$ has $E^\circ = +1.36\text{ V}$. The reduction $\text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cl}^- + 2\text{OH}^-$ has $E^\circ = +0.89\text{ V}$.

Subtract to get the overall cell**
The more positive electrode stays as reduction, the less positive is reversed as oxidation. So: $$E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode} - E^\circ_{anode} = 1.36 - 0.89 = +0.47\text{ V}$$ A positive value tells you the disproportionation in alkali is feasible under standard conditions.
Final answer: $E^\circ(\text{Cl}_2/\text{Cl}^-) = +1.36\text{ V}$ and $E^\circ(\text{ClO}^-/\text{Cl}^-) = +0.89\text{ V}$\n$$E^\circ_{cell} = 1.36 - 0.89 = +0.47\text{ V}$$

hints: Look at the overall equilibrium $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ and ask which side $\text{OH}^-$ appears on.
Apply Le Chatelier to increased $[\text{OH}^-]$ to predict whether the forward reaction is driven further and whether the cell potential becomes more or less positive.
walkthrough:
See $E^\circ$ as standard only**
$E^\circ_{cell}$ assumes all ions at $1.00\text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. As soon as you raise $[\text{OH}^-]$, you are no longer standard, so the measured $E_{cell}$ will shift.

Apply Le Chatelier**
In $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cl}^- + \text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\text{OH}^-$ is a reactant. Raising its concentration pushes the equilibrium to the right to use up the extra $\text{OH}^-$.

Link position of equilibrium to $E_{cell}$**
A greater drive to the right means a greater driving force for the cell reaction, so the measured $E_{cell}$ becomes more positive than the standard $+0.47\text{ V}$. You can also view it as the $\text{ClO}^-/\text{Cl}^-$ half cell containing $\text{OH}^-$ being perturbed.

Final answer: $E_{cell}$ becomes more positive than $E^\circ_{cell}$ (third box ticked).\nIncreasing $[\text{OH}^-]$ increases reactant concentration so equilibrium shifts to the right, driving the forward reaction further and increasing $E_{cell}$.

hints: Write the two alkaline reductions involved, $\text{ClO}^-/\text{Cl}^-$ with $E^\circ = +0.89\text{ V}$ and $\text{BrO}_3^-/\text{Br}^-$ with $E^\circ = +0.58\text{ V}$, and decide which is reversed as oxidation.
walkthrough:
Combine reduction with reversed oxidation**
$\text{ClO}^-$ is the stronger oxidant ($+0.89\text{ V}$) so it stays as reduction: $\text{ClO}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \text{Cl}^- + 2\text{OH}^-$. The bromate half equation $\text{BrO}_3^- + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} + 6e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Br}^- + 6\text{OH}^-$ must run backwards as oxidation. Multiplying the chlorate(I) reduction by 3 to balance 6 electrons and cancelling $3\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $6\text{OH}^-$ gives $\text{Br}^- + 3\text{ClO}^- \longrightarrow \text{BrO}_3^- + 3\text{Cl}^-$.

hints: Use $E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ$ (oxidant, $\text{ClO}^-$) minus $E^\circ$ (reductant system, $\text{BrO}_3^-$) with $+0.89\text{ V}$ and $+0.58\text{ V}$.
walkthrough:
Subtract the half cell values**
The cathode is the more positive $\text{ClO}^-/\text{Cl}^-$ couple. So $$E^\circ_{cell} = +0.89 - (+0.58) = +0.31\text{ V}$$ The positive sign confirms $\text{ClO}^-$ can feasibly oxidise $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{BrO}_3^-$ in alkali.

hints: Assign oxidation numbers in $\text{HBrO}_3$, $\text{Br}_2$, $\text{O}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to see that Br(+5) is reduced to Br(0) while O(-2) is oxidised to O(0).
walkthrough:
Balance by oxidation number**
In $\text{HBrO}_3$, Br is +5 and O is -2. Products allowed are $\text{Br}_2$ where Br is 0 (reduction, gain of 5 electrons per Br) and $\text{O}_2$ where O is 0 (oxidation, loss of 2 electrons per O). Balancing electron gain and loss with H and O atoms gives $4\text{HBrO}_3 \longrightarrow 2\text{Br}_2 + 5\text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Check: 4 H, 4 Br and 12 O on each side.
